title: Buddhism Comes to China
objective: After this level you can explain how Buddhism changed in China into Chan (Zen) and Pure Land, and how the "three teachings" came to share one household.
summary: Buddhism reached China with merchants in the late Han, adapted to family values, and grew Chan (Zen) and Pure Land. Beside Confucianism and Daoism it became one of the 'three teachings'.

cards.headline: "Buddhism is the sun, Daoism the moon, Confucianism the five planets."
cards.body: A 6th-century Chinese scholar wrote that. How did a teaching from outside China come to share its sky?

cards.headline: Arriving with merchants
cards.body: Buddhism began to enter China as a religion of foreign merchants in the later years of the Han dynasty. Early translators rendered "sutra" as jing, the word already used for the Confucian and Daoist classics. A borrowed word was a kind of welcome: Buddhist texts arrived sounding like classics.

cards.headline: Monks in a family culture
cards.body: To some in China, celibate monks and nuns seemed to threaten family values. Buddhism made room for the family. Monastics used kinship terms for one another, and monks and lay donors held rituals to comfort the ancestors. Level 62's filial piety didn't shut Buddhism out; it changed how Buddhism was lived.

cards.headline: Meditation and a name
cards.body: In China two schools took shape. Chan means "Meditation", from the Sanskrit dhyana; in Japanese it's Zen. It calls itself "a special transmission outside the scriptures", pointing straight at the mind. Pure Land devotees call on the name of Amitabha Buddha, hoping to be reborn in his Western Paradise, the Pure Land. One sits in silence; the other calls a name.

cards.headline: Three teachings, one household
cards.body: The Chinese came to speak of sanjiao, the "three teachings": Confucianism, Daoism and Buddhism. Li Shiqian's sun, moon and planets put all three in one sky. Remember Level 2's Confucian scholar at a Daoist or Buddhist ritual? Following one tradition didn't demand total commitment to it alone.

cards.headline: Buddhism Comes to China: the takeaways
learned: Buddhism entered China with merchants in the late Han
Chan (Zen) stresses meditation; Pure Land calls on Amitabha
Sanjiao: three teachings sharing one sky

questions.prompt: What does the Chinese Buddhist name Chan mean?

options.label: Honoring the ancestors
options.rationale: Chan names a practice, not a relative.

questions.explanation: Chan comes from the Sanskrit dhyana, "meditation", and is called Zen in Japanese.

questions.prompt: How did Buddhism adapt to China's family-centered culture?

options.label: Monks and nuns were required to marry
Monastics used kinship terms and held rituals to comfort the ancestors
Temples were built only inside family homes, never as separate buildings

questions.explanation: Buddhism made room for family values: kinship terms among monastics and rites for the ancestors.

questions.prompt: Level 8 said East Asians may call themselves Daoists or Buddhists yet seldom stop being Confucians. Which idea from this level fits that?

options.label: The rendering of sutra as jing
Buddhism's arrival with merchants
options.rationale: That's about how it came, not how it's combined.

options.label: Sanjiao: three teachings sharing one sky

questions.explanation: Seen as three teachings in one sky, the traditions could be followed together rather than chosen between.
